title: Fed Governor Waller: Need to get a little more aggressive in our rate hikes to tame inflation
summary: On CNBC's Squawk Box, Fed Governor Christopher Waller tells Steve Liesman he is very worried that inflation is moving the wrong way and spreading beyond energy as businesses pass higher costs on to customers. He argues the Fed should first reverse the three insurance cuts it made in 2025 and may need to go further, and says a half-point increase at the December meeting would be better than a quarter point plus a hint about January. His aim, he explains, is to jolt households and firms out of treating roughly three per cent inflation as the new normal, even though markets had mostly expected a smaller move.
focus: Shadow the stretch where Waller explains why he would rather do a single half-point hike in December than a smaller move with a signal about January, and the short passage where he describes inflation spreading beyond energy, since both model calm, conditional policy reasoning.

vocab.meaning: the degree to which a business's higher costs are passed on to customers as higher prices
vocab.context: Waller said companies pushing their rising costs onto shoppers is a key reason he wants the Fed to act more forcefully.
vocab.example: Our pricing review found near-full pass-through of freight costs in the grocery segment but almost none in apparel.

vocab.meaning: to fix expectations or beliefs firmly around a particular level
vocab.context: He worried that the public has started to treat roughly three per cent inflation as normal and build its plans around that figure.
vocab.example: If the board anchors on last year's 20% growth, any realistic target will look like a failure.

vocab.meaning: to cause something that had calmed down to start again, often more strongly
vocab.context: The coverage explained that the conflict involving Iran and shipping limits in the Strait of Hormuz pushed energy costs up and brought inflation back.
vocab.example: A single price cut by the new entrant could reignite the discounting war we spent two years ending.

vocab.meaning: to continue to exist or have an effect for longer than expected
vocab.context: The report noted that the effects of earlier tariffs have stayed in the system, helping keep most inflation measures above three per cent.
vocab.example: Integration costs from the acquisition are likely to linger well into the second year.

vocab.meaning: happening or changing at a particular time of year in a regular pattern
vocab.context: Petrol prices were described as easing because of normal autumn patterns, though still higher than before the war.
vocab.example: Strip out the seasonal uplift from Black Friday before you compare November with October.

vocab.meaning: happening slowly and in small steps rather than suddenly
vocab.context: Some other Fed officials were reported to prefer a slower, step-by-step series of rate increases rather than a big move.
vocab.example: We recommend a gradual price increase over three quarters to limit churn among smaller accounts.

vocab.meaning: existing or happening before a particular war started
vocab.context: Fuel costs were compared with where they stood before the conflict began, and were still above that level.
vocab.example: Shipping rates on the Asia–Europe lane have still not returned to pre-war levels.

vocab.meaning: to surprise people suddenly and strongly so that they change their view or behaviour
vocab.zh: 使震惊；（以出人意料之举）震动
vocab.context: Waller argued that a bigger-than-expected move might be needed to jolt people out of assuming inflation will stay high.
vocab.example: Sometimes you have to shock the organisation with a hard deadline before people take the restructuring seriously.

vocab.meaning: one hundredth of one percentage point, used to describe changes in interest rates or yields
vocab.context: Waller talked about raising rates by fifty of these units in December instead of the twenty-five that markets expected.
vocab.example: Refinancing now would save the client about 80 basis points on its term loan.

vocab.meaning: the main short-term interest rate that a central bank sets to steer the economy
vocab.context: He said the level the Fed's key rate had been at was clearly not strong enough to bring prices down.
vocab.example: The client's FX hedging strategy assumes the central bank's policy rate peaks early next year.

vocab.meaning: an interest-rate reduction made as a precaution against a possible slowdown, not because the economy is already weak
vocab.context: Waller said the Fed first needs to reverse the precautionary cuts it made in 2025 before going any further.
vocab.example: Management treated the hiring freeze as an insurance cut to costs in case the second-half order book weakened.

vocab.meaning: a central bank's public signals about where interest rates are likely to go in future
vocab.context: The coverage noted that Fed Chair Warsh dislikes signalling future moves, and Waller said he would rather act now than hint at a January increase.
vocab.example: Investors punished the stock because the CFO offered no forward guidance on margins for next year.

phrases.meaning: (of financial markets) to reflect an expected future event in current prices before it happens
phrases.context: Futures markets were described as already assuming a quarter-point increase in December was highly likely.
phrases.example: The share price already prices in a successful product launch, so there is little upside left.

phrases.meaning: to stay above the normal or target level, especially of inflation or an economy
phrases.zh: （通胀/经济）持续偏高；过热运行
phrases.context: The reporting described inflation as staying above the Fed's goal for an extended period.
phrases.example: Labour costs have been running hot in the Gulf region, so we have budgeted a 9% wage uplift.

phrases.zh: 朝错误的方向发展；每况愈下
phrases.context: Waller used this idea to describe inflation moving further away from the Fed's target and spreading beyond energy.
phrases.example: Customer satisfaction scores are headed in the wrong direction, and the churn data will follow.

phrases.meaning: to reverse an earlier action or decision
phrases.context: He said the Fed must undo the three rate cuts from 2025, and possibly go further than that.
phrases.example: If input costs fall next year, we may have to take back part of this price increase to stay competitive.
